summary: I'm an AI/ML Engineer and M.Tech researcher at IIT Tirupati (IIT ISM Dhanbad alumnus), working at the intersection of generative modelling, financial ML, and production-ready AI systems. My current focus: making generative models actually useful, not just visually convincing. Recent work that defines how I think: Trained Diffusion Models and TimeGAN on financial time series to generate synthetic stock data. Diffusion looked perfect. TimeGAN won on predictive performance. That gap between visual realism and temporal logic is now the core question driving my research. Building RAG systems that go beyond basic retrieval, exploring chunking strategies, embedding choices, vector search, and evaluation frameworks to make LLM applications genuinely reliable in production. Built Finsphere, a React Native fintech application integrating mobile banking, microfinance, and digital insurance, because good AI needs good infrastructure around it.What I care about: Most people in this space optimise for what looks impressive. I optimise for what actually works when tested on real data, real users, and real constraints. That means being honest when a model fails. Building systems end-to-end. And asking better questions before writing a single line of code.What I'm exploring next: Hybrid generative architectures that combine Diffusion's global smoothness with TimeGAN's temporal coherence, and whether that unlocks better synthetic data for downstream forecasting.If you're working on a problem where AI needs to be reliable, not just impressive, I'd like to hear about it. DM me or connect here.

Since my M.Sc. dissertation, I've been studying landslides in the Sikkim Himalaya, and my M.Tech thesis at IIT (ISM) Dhanbad returned to that terrain with a harder toolkit: comparing classical, ensemble, and deep-learning susceptibility models against one another, then testing their predictions against PSInSAR displacement time series from Sentinel-1. A susceptibility map is a static claim about a landscape that isn't static. Closing that gap is what interests me because it's what must happen before a hazard map can warn anyone. Before the M.Tech I spent two and a half years as a GIS Analyst with the Government of West Bengal, working on watershed development under PMKSY-WDC 2.0. The maps I made there went to administrators deciding where to spend money, not to journals. That changed what I think a model is for. I also work on the human side of spatial analysis. With colleagues in Midnapore, I co-authored a Springer book on using GIS to improve health outcomes in urban slums, and I continue to publish on healthcare access, urban heat, land-use change, and groundwater potential.
